headline: Falling house prices and declining transactions are a normal property cycle, not an exceptional macro shock — the budget and interest rates are not the culprits, lender discipline is
reasoning: Andrews explicitly distances the current property downturn from macro policy failures, noting that the Treasurer and RBA Governor 'have never approved a loan.' The slowdown in house prices and transaction volumes is characterised as a routine cyclical event that experienced lenders have navigated many times before. The stress being observed is a function of lender behaviour during the prior upcycle, not an unusual macroeconomic deterioration.
quote: You're not pointing the finger at the budget. You're not pointing at rising interest rates. You know, it's still soft. Jim Chalmers and Michelle Bullock, to my knowledge, have never approved a loan. So what we're seeing is a normal property cycle. And we're seeing which managers are well prepared for it and which managers are not.

headline: Regulatory scrutiny from ASIC and APRA acting as a clearing mechanism, with survivors likely to be higher-quality, better-governed operators
reasoning: Chris Andrews argues that the current period of regulatory pressure from ASIC and APRA is a healthy 'tide going out' moment for Australian private credit. ASIC has spent the last two years focused on governance, hygiene and transparency, and has recently signalled active surveillance and enforcement. Andrews believes this ongoing regulatory process benefits high-quality operators — managers, investors and borrowers alike — by creating a well-regulated, transparent sector where investors can properly assess risks and compare managers. He views this as a necessary clearing-out that will ultimately strengthen the sector's credibility.
quote: That's what we're happening now. We'll have a little bit of a clearing out in the sector. ASIC, I think over the last two years has been rightly focused on a whole lot of issues of good governance, good hygiene, transparency in this sector. That process will be ongoing. They gave a really strong speech yesterday, pointing to a number of surveillance activities that they're conducting, some enforcement actions that they've got on foot. So it sounds like ASIC hasn't missed a beat on this, which is important for the industry because for any high quality operator in the sector, Nadine, I'm saying whether you're a manager, whether you're an investor or on the other side of the balance sheet, if you're a borrower, what we want is a well regulated, transparent sector where an investor can come in, properly assess the risks, properly compare managers to, which has been something that's been really difficult over the last few years.

headline: Well-prepared private credit managers with diversified first-mortgage portfolios, strong liquidity frameworks and transparency will navigate the current property downturn without major stress; poorly prepared managers with concentrated developer exposure and weak liquidity controls face the real risk
reasoning: Andrews argues the current property cycle stress is not a systemic private credit crisis but a normal cyclical downturn exposing lenders with poor practices. He identifies four hallmarks of a well-prepared manager: high-quality first senior mortgage assets, a broadly diversified loan portfolio (not 10-50 concentrated loans), appropriate liquidity frameworks committed to investor redemption terms, and full transparency via publicly available portfolio disclosures updated monthly. He warns that 'bad loans are written in good times' and that managers overexposed to individual developers with poor leverage and cash-flow disciplines are now facing consequences. ASIC surveillance and enforcement actions are ongoing, which he views as a positive clearing-out for the sector overall.
quote: As a lender, you are always preparing for a downturn. Or at least you should be. And our concern is we're looking at the market now is there seems to be what is a pretty straightforward situation where a developer in the western suburbs of Sydney has gotten itself into trouble... bad loans are written in good times. So when you look at a situation where you've got a slowing property market, what you do see is those lenders who've been building really good quality, diversified portfolios around high quality assets. They won't have any trouble at all. They may have a few extra borrowers go into difficulty. They'll work through those and come out the other end, in really good shape for those lenders who've been overexposed to poor, poor practices of lending to individual developers who haven't been keeping their disciplines around their exposures to leverage, around cash flow and those sorts of things.

headline: ASIC surveillance and enforcement actions are a net positive — the sector will emerge stronger after a clearing-out, with better governance and transparency standards
reasoning: Andrews welcomes the heightened ASIC scrutiny, noting the regulator has been focused for two years on governance, hygiene and transparency in private credit. A recent ASIC speech flagged ongoing surveillance activities and enforcement actions. He believes this regulatory pressure, combined with market stress exposing weak managers, will produce a healthier and more credible private credit sector, benefiting disciplined managers and their investors over the cycle.
quote: ASIC, I think over the last two years has been rightly focused on a whole lot of issues of good governance, good hygiene, transparency in this sector. That process will be ongoing. They gave a really strong speech yesterday, pointing to a number of surveillance activities that they're conducting, some enforcement actions that they've got on foot. So it sounds like ASIC hasn't missed a beat on this, which is important.

headline: La Trobe Financial deploying $1.5bn per month into Australian residential and commercial mortgages, describing the strategy as domestic private credit
reasoning: Chris Andrews notes that La Trobe's existing Australian portfolios are performing very well, with roughly $1.5 billion per month being deployed into residential and commercial mortgages. He observes that what is now labelled 'private credit' is essentially the same asset class La Trobe has operated in for decades. He is comfortable with the exposure and dismisses concern about label-driven categorisation, emphasising the importance of focusing on underlying portfolio fundamentals.
quote: We in terms of our existing portfolios, Andrew, they're performing really well. So we're deploying about 1.5 billion a month into, you know, residential and commercial mortgages here in Australia. These days, people call that private credit. Ten years ago no one was calling a private credit. So, you know, in terms of that exposure, we're very comfortable with that.

He expects consistent inflows to continue and plans to leverage scale advantages — including access to high quality deal flow, broader liquidity management, and technology investment — to benefit investors further.

We all know Australia's population, like the rest of the world, is getting older on average over time. And as investors age, as investors approach retirement, they need consistent capital, stable, reliable type income sources. So we've been producing that for many decades.
